Osama Bin Laden's written propaganda targeted young men in Muslim countries with grievances against the West, and marginalized Muslims living in the West; it framed him as a leader against Western imperialism and invoked global jihad. #bin_laden_propaganda

Bin Laden's most effective propaganda mediums were video and audio recordings (e.g., first post-9/11 video aired on Al Jazeera Oct 7, 2001, timed with the US invasion of Afghanistan), plus internet forums and social media to reach young, tech-savvy audiences. #bin_laden_propaganda

Bin Laden did not target non-Muslim audiences; his propaganda was aimed at Muslims and rooted in Islamic religious tradition, portraying the West as a Crusader threat to Muslim identity. #bin_laden_propaganda

Bin Laden's propaganda affected Muslim-country politics by recruiting followers in Afghanistan, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, inspiring groups like Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula and Boko Haram, and fueling anti-Western rhetoric and stricter security/civil-liberty restrictions. #bin_laden_propaganda

Muslim scholars and leaders who spoke out against Bin Laden's extremism include the Grand Mufti of Saudi Arabia, Tariq Ramadan and Sheikh Hamza Yusuf; they argued terrorism against civilians violates Islamic principles. #bin_laden_propaganda

Attacks cited as influenced by Bin Laden's propaganda: 9/11 (2001), Madrid train bombings (2004, attackers left a video referencing Bin Laden), London 7/7 bombings (2005, 52 killed), Bali bombings (2002, 200+ killed) and the 2004 Australian Embassy bombing in Jakarta. #bin_laden_propaganda

Triggers of Bin Laden's anti-West propaganda campaign: US troops stationed in Saudi Arabia, the 1991 US-led Gulf War, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, and the 2001 US-led invasion of Afghanistan. #bin_laden_propaganda
